intro: Day one of twenty-three: before any single site, the shape of the whole journey. Egypt, Sinai, the land and the far bank of the Jordan trace the Exodus, and the trip ends where Moses ended, looking west from Nebo.

stories.headline: A route drawn in the shape of Exodus
stories.dek: Twelve days cross a river kingdom, a granite massif, a rain-fed ridge and a rift valley, and the land itself teaches the difference between Egypt and Canaan.
body: Lay the itinerary on a relief map and it stops looking like a tour. It starts at sea level in a river valley, climbs into the granite of southern Sinai, drops to the Gulf of Aqaba, runs north up a rift valley, climbs again to the ridge of Bethlehem and Jerusalem, goes down below sea level to Galilee, and finishes on the plateau east of the Jordan looking back across the water. Egypt, wilderness, the land, and the far bank: the order of Exodus to Deuteronomy, walked mostly in the right direction, with one deliberate twist at the end.

That twist is the point to hold onto. Israel entered from the east, crossing the Jordan westward under Joshua. This group leaves eastward across the Jordan and ends on Mount Nebo, standing where Moses stood. The pilgrimage closes not in possession but in a view. Every other day of the trip should be read in the light of that last morning.
## Two kinds of water

The single most useful geographical text for the whole trip is Deuteronomy 11:10–12. Moses tells Israel that the land they are entering is not like Egypt, where you sowed seed and "watered it with your foot", working irrigation channels fed by the Nile. Canaan is a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from heaven, a land the LORD's eyes are on from the beginning of the year to its end. Egypt's agriculture depended on a river that rose every year whatever anyone believed; the hill country depended on rain that might not come. Geography became a school of trust. (The Dagon's Coast note already covers Deuteronomy 11:14 and the question of who gives the grain; this edition stays with the contrast of water systems.)

The group will feel this contrast physically. On Day 3, driving out of Cairo, watch for the hard line where irrigated green stops and desert starts, sometimes within a few metres. The Egyptians called their country Kemet, the black land of Nile silt, and the desert Deshret, the red land. Since the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970 the annual flood no longer comes, but the edge of the black land is still visible from the bus. By Day 5, in Israel, the pilgrims enter a world where everything depends on winter rain, and they arrive in the middle of it.
## The spine of the trip: one long crack

From Day 4 onward almost every road follows or crosses a single geological feature: the rift that runs from the Gulf of Aqaba through the Arabah, the Dead Sea basin, the Jordan Valley and up to the Sea of Galilee. It is a transform boundary between the Arabian and African plates, and it is the reason the land has such violent contrasts of height in such short distances. The lowest dry ground on earth lies in this trench (the Dead Sea note has the numbers and the theology). The Sea of Galilee sits roughly 210 metres below sea level in the same trough.

Two consequences matter for the pilgrim. First, heights change fast. The road from the Dead Sea basin up to Jerusalem climbs well over a kilometre in roughly 35 to 40 kilometres; ears pop and temperatures fall by ten degrees or more in under an hour. Second, the central ridge acts as a rain wall. Winter storms from the Mediterranean drop their rain on the western slopes; a short drive east of Bethlehem the land turns to the bare, chalky Judean wilderness. Standing in Bethlehem on Day 5, the group is on the watershed: rain that falls on one side of town flows to the Mediterranean, on the other side to the Dead Sea.
## A narrow bridge between empires

Rainey and Notley's atlas The Sacred Bridge reads the southern Levant as a corridor squeezed between the sea and the desert, the only practical land route between the river civilisations of Egypt and Mesopotamia. That is why the same small country appears in Egyptian, Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Greek and Roman records, and why the Holy Family could flee to Egypt along a road that empires had worn smooth. When pilgrims ask why so much history happened in a place so small, the answer is that the land is a hallway, not a room.
## Late December on the ground

Expect three climates. Cairo and the Red Sea coast are mild by day; nights in the Sinai highlands around St Catherine's can approach freezing, and Jerusalem and Bethlehem in December are typically cool and wet, with long-run averages roughly in the 6 to 13°C range (approximate climate normals; check the actual forecast 72 hours out). The Dead Sea and Jericho are warm in comparison, so layers come off on Day 6 and go back on that night. Petra and Nebo on the Transjordan plateau can be cold and windy, and the Siq is a flash-flood channel when it rains on the plateau. Daylight is short: sunset falls roughly between 16:40 and 17:40 local time depending on the country, so outdoor sites must be front-loaded into the morning.
## What to look for on the road

Point out five things. The black-land edge outside Cairo (Day 3). The red and grey granite of southern Sinai, ancient basement rock very different from the limestone of Judea (Day 4). The straight, walled trough of the Arabah north of the Gulf, with the mountains of Edom to the east (Day 5). The sudden switch from green terraces to desert as you look east from the Bethlehem ridge (Days 5 to 7). And the view west from Nebo across the Jordan Valley to the Judean hills on the last morning (Day 11), on a clear day as far as the Bethlehem ridge.
stories.why: A group that understands the shape of the land stops collecting sites and starts reading a story. For the pastor, Deuteronomy 11 gives a framework that can be recalled at almost every stop: a river you control versus rain you must receive. It also sets up the closing service at Nebo as the true end of the arc rather than a detour on the way to the airport.
questions: Where in your own life do you prefer an irrigation system you can control to rain you must wait for?
If the trip ends with a view rather than an arrival, how should that change what you expect the next twelve days to give you?
Which of the five landscape features would you most want the group to notice, and how will you stop the bus long enough for them to see it?

stories.headline: Two thousand years of reading the land
stories.dek: Christians have argued since the second century about whether the places of Scripture teach anything the text does not, and both sides of the argument belong on the bus.
body: Every pilgrim group meets the phrase sooner or later: the land is the fifth gospel. It sounds like a modern brochure line, but the idea is old, its most famous formulation is French and sceptical, and the church has always held it alongside a strong warning. Knowing that history protects a group from two errors at once: treating the sites as magic, and treating them as decoration.
## The first Christian visitors came for the Bible

The earliest Christian traveller we can name went east to settle a question about Scripture, not to see relics. Eusebius preserves a letter in which Melito, bishop of Sardis around AD 170, tells his friend Onesimus that when he went east he learned accurately the books of the Old Testament, and he lists them (Church History 4.26.13–14). Esther is missing from his list. Origen, a generation later, used his own travels to argue about readings in the Gospels, for example preferring Bethabara to Bethany in John 1:28 on the basis of what he heard in the region. From the start, Christian travel to the land served the reading of texts.

Jerome, who lived in Bethlehem from the 380s, put the principle most memorably in his preface to the Books of Chronicles: just as those who have seen Athens understand Greek history better, so whoever has seen Judea with their own eyes reads Scripture more clearly. (Constantine's building programme, Helena's visit, the Bordeaux Pilgrim and Egeria are already covered in the Holy Sepulchre, Via Dolorosa, Taba and Suez notes and are not repeated here.)
## The warning came at the same time

The same century produced the sharpest criticism of pilgrimage in Christian history. Gregory of Nyssa, who had been to Jerusalem on church business, travelling by the imperial post, wrote a letter (his Letter 2, usually titled On Pilgrimages) arguing that the Lord never listed a journey to Jerusalem among the things that lead to the kingdom. Change of place, he wrote, does not effect any drawing nearer to God. He worried about the moral dangers of the road and concluded that his own Cappadocia, with its many altars, was no less holy. He would rather Christians left the body to go to the Lord than left Cappadocia to go to Palestine.

Jerome, despite living in Bethlehem, said something similar to Paulinus of Nola in Letter 58. What deserves praise is not having been at Jerusalem but having lived a good life there. The courts of heaven are as open from Britain as from Jerusalem. Antony and the great monks of Egypt never saw Jerusalem, and the door of paradise opened to them anyway. The two strongest advocates for reading the land were also its most honest critics.
## Renan's torn gospel

The exact phrase comes from Ernest Renan. After leading a French scientific mission to Phoenicia in 1860 and 1861, and travelling through Galilee, Samaria and Judea, he wrote in the introduction to his Vie de Jésus (1863) that he had seen "a fifth gospel, torn but still legible" (un cinquième Évangile, lacéré, mais lisible encore). For Renan the land helped explain Jesus as a gentle Galilean moralist shaped by his landscape, not as the incarnate Son. The phrase was born inside a project to make the Gospels less supernatural. That should make a preacher careful about using it uncritically.

Later Christian scholars reclaimed it. The Benedictine archaeologist Bargil Pixner, who lived for decades by the Sea of Galilee, titled his guide With Jesus through Galilee according to the Fifth Gospel, using the land to strengthen rather than dissolve confidence in the Gospel accounts. The Theology Note Jesus and the Logic of History already flags a different danger under the same name: the "fifth gospel" of scholarly reconstruction that mirrors the scholar. The land can become that kind of fifth gospel too, if a guide's story replaces the text.
## The modern pilgrimage industry

Mass pilgrimage as the group will experience it is a nineteenth-century creation. Edward Robinson and Eli Smith's survey of 1838 used Arabic village names to identify biblical places and founded scientific biblical geography. Mark Twain's satirical Innocents Abroad (1869) mocked the first American package excursion of 1867, and Thomas Cook began conducted tours of Palestine around the same years. Many sites the group visits rest on three different kinds of claim: places fixed by geography that cannot move (the lake, the Jordan, the Mount of Olives); places identified by early Christian memory that predates Constantine (the Bethlehem cave, Golgotha); and places chosen later for devotional convenience (several Via Dolorosa stations, some Galilee chapels). A useful habit for the whole trip is to tell the group which kind each site is.
## How authenticity debates should sound on this trip

The fair position is neither credulous nor cynical. Where a tradition is early and continuous, say so and say why it matters. Where a site is a commemoration rather than a location, say that too; commemoration is an honest and ancient Christian practice. Gregory and Jerome supply the guardrail: the value of standing somewhere is that it sends you back to the text and to Christ, not that the place transmits holiness by contact.
stories.why: Pilgrims will hear the fifth-gospel line from guides, and some will expect the land to deliver experiences the Scriptures do not promise. Knowing that the church held both enthusiasm and suspicion from the fourth century lets the pastor bless the trip without overselling it. It also gives a simple, repeatable classification of sites that keeps the group honest when authenticity is debated.
questions: Is Gregory of Nyssa's warning a criticism of what you are about to do, or a description of how to do it well?
When a guide says the land is a fifth gospel, what would you want the group to hear you add?
Which sites on the itinerary do you expect to be geography, which early memory, and which later devotion?

stories.headline: Guests in a land others call home
stories.dek: The biblical world knew how to treat the traveller and the stranger; the group is about to be both, among Copts, Jews, Muslims, Bedouin and Arab Christians.
body: The Bible was largely written by and for people who travelled on foot in groups. That world had rules for strangers, songs for the road and assumptions about family that shaped how a journey worked. The group will be travellers in that same land, but this time as guests of communities who live there now. Both halves deserve attention before departure.
## A culture that sang on the road

Israel's law required pilgrimage: three times a year every male was to appear before the LORD at the place he would choose (Deuteronomy 16:16). The Psalter preserves a small travel songbook, Psalms 120 to 134, each headed "a song of ascents", most likely sung on the climb to Jerusalem. They begin far from home ("woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech", Psalm 120:5), pass through danger on the road and end in the temple at night (Psalm 134). Reading one ascent psalm each morning on the bus from Day 5 onward is a simple way to let the group pray the way the first pilgrims did.

Pilgrims travelled in large kin groups. Luke 2:41–45 shows the scale: Mary and Joseph travelled a full day assuming the twelve-year-old Jesus was somewhere in the company (Greek synodia, a travelling party). Nobody counted. The Western Wall note lists the temple scene; the detail for a tour leader is the caravan. Extended-family travel made it normal not to see a child for hours, and it took three days to find him. Every TL on this route lives inside that verse.
## Strangers protected by law

In the world of the text, the ger, the resident outsider, had almost no natural protector, so the Torah made God his protector. Israel was told to love the sojourner because they had been sojourners in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:18–19), and God said of the land itself that it was his and that Israel were sojourners and settlers with him (Leviticus 25:23). Hospitality to a stranger was an honour obligation; failing it shamed the household. Receiving hospitality carried obligations too: to accept what is offered, to praise the host, not to criticise the house. Pilgrims who refuse tea in a Bethlehem shop or comment loudly on a host's poverty are breaking a code their own Bible assumes.
## The communities the group will meet

Egypt. In Old Cairo and Mokattam the group will be among Coptic Orthodox Christians, the largest Christian community in the Middle East. Copts keep Christmas on 7 January and observe a long Nativity Fast before it, which begins in late November; during the group's Egypt days many Copts will be eating no meat or dairy. Do not offer food that breaks a fast to Coptic hosts, and do not describe their Christmas as late.

Israel. Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics counted about 185,000 Christians at the end of 2025, about 1.9 percent of the population, and nearly 80 percent of them Arab. Nazareth and Haifa each have roughly 19,000 Arab Christians and Jerusalem about 13,400 (JNS reporting of CBS figures, December 2025). The group will meet Jewish Israelis at borders, in Galilee and in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter, where Shabbat runs from Friday sunset; on Christmas Day, a Friday this year, observance begins in the late afternoon.

Palestine. Bethlehem, where the group sleeps three nights, is a Muslim-majority city with an old, shrinking Christian community whose economy depends on pilgrims. In December 2025 the city lit its Christmas tree in Manger Square for the first time since the Gaza war began; the mayor said unemployment had risen from 14 to 65 percent, about 4,000 people had left to find work, and around 80 percent of residents live off tourism (Times of Israel, 7 December 2025). A group sleeping in Bethlehem at Christmas is an economic event for families there.

Jordan and Sinai. In Sinai the group will meet Bedouin guides and camel handlers; in Jordan, a Muslim-majority kingdom with long-established Arab Christian communities and the custodians of the Baptism Site and Nebo. Jordan prides itself on hospitality; accepting coffee is part of the visit.
## How to honour them

Five habits cover most of it. Greet before you photograph, and ask before photographing people, especially women and Bedouin. Buy from local Christian shops in Bethlehem and Nazareth rather than only at the coach stop; that is the most direct help a pilgrim can give. Keep political arguments off the bus and out of shops; Indonesia has no diplomatic relations with Israel, and the group will hear strong views from every side. Never stage worship or evangelism at Jewish or Muslim holy places. And refer to people by the names they use for themselves: Copts, Palestinian Christians, Arab Israelis, Bedouin. The Abu Sirga note covers the Coptic tradition of the Holy Family; this edition only asks the group to meet the Copts as a church, not as a backdrop.
stories.why: The biblical world gives the group a script for being guests: honour the host, protect the stranger, travel as a body. For the pastor, the communities along the route are fellow members of Christ's body living under pressure, and a pilgrimage that ignores them turns the land into a museum. The Luke 2 caravan is also the single best image for explaining why the TL counts heads.
questions: How would Deuteronomy 10:19 change the way the group behaves when it is the stranger rather than the host?
What would it look like for this group's spending in Bethlehem to be an act of fellowship rather than shopping?
Which ascent psalm would you assign to which day, and why?

stories.headline: Strangers in the land they were promised
stories.dek: Hebrews says Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner and died having only greeted the promise from afar, which is the most honest description of a pilgrimage in the Bible.
body: Hermeneutical lens: Canonical-Intertextual. Hebrews 11:8–16 is a dense reading of Genesis 12 to 25 through the Greek Old Testament, and its key words echo Genesis 23, Leviticus 25, Psalm 39 and 1 Chronicles 29. It interprets the whole trip.
## Obeying while the call is still sounding (v. 8)

Verse 8 says Abraham obeyed "when he was called", but the Greek participle is present (kaloumenos): he obeyed while being called, as the call was still sounding. And he went out "not knowing where he was going". The pilgrims hold a printed itinerary; Abraham had none. A tour with a run sheet is not faith; what makes it a pilgrimage is the willingness to be led into what the run sheet cannot predict.
## A foreigner in the promised land (vv. 9–10)

Verse 9 is the surprise. Abraham "sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land" (paroikēsen eis gēn tēs epangelias hōs allotrian). The verb paroikeō is the Septuagint's standard way of rendering the Hebrew gur, to live as a ger, a resident alien. Abraham did not merely pass through on the way to the promise; he lived in the promised land itself as an outsider, in tents, with Isaac and Jacob. Verse 10 gives the reason: he was waiting for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder (technitēs kai dēmiourgos) is God. Abraham's only purchased property in Canaan was a grave (Genesis 23), bought while calling himself "a sojourner and foreigner among you" (Genesis 23:4).
## Seeing and greeting from afar (v. 13)

Verse 13 is the centre. They all died in faith without receiving what was promised, "having seen them and greeted them from afar." The verb aspazomai is the ordinary word for greeting someone; Lane (WBC 47B) reads it as the greeting of travellers who sight a destination they have not reached. The patriarchs then "acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth" (xenoi kai parepidēmoi). That phrase is built from Genesis 23:4 in the Greek Bible (paroikos kai parepidēmos), and it is echoed in David's prayer, "we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15), and in Psalm 39:12. (See the Elect Exiles draft for parepidēmos in 1 Peter 1:1.)

There is a real exegetical crux in the last two words, epi tēs gēs. Gē can mean the earth or the land. But Genesis 23 and Leviticus 25:23 are about the land: Abraham confessed he was a stranger in Canaan, and God told Israel the land is his and they are sojourners and settlers with him. The pilgrims will stand in the very land the confession was made in, and the confession still holds there.
## A homeland behind or ahead (vv. 14–16)

People who speak like this, verse 14 says, are seeking a homeland (patris). If they had been thinking of the country they left, Ur or Haran, they had opportunity to return. Their exile was chosen. Verse 16 names what they wanted: a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Heavenly (epouraniou) in Hebrews does not mean immaterial; it names where God's purposes are already real (12:22: the heavenly Jerusalem, Mount Zion). Bound for the Promised Land already traces the land as a type of the new creation; Hebrews 11 says the patriarchs themselves read it that way.

Then the honour statement: "Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city." deSilva's socio-rhetorical commentary (Perseverance in Gratitude) shows how the author uses honour language throughout: those who accept low status in the world's eyes are the ones God publicly owns. The line looks back to the bush, where God introduced himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6); The Fire That Sends note covers that scene, and Hebrews here explains why God attaches his name to wanderers.
## The Christological centre

Hebrews does not leave the pilgrimage with Abraham. Jesus is the pioneer and perfecter of faith (12:2), who went before the people; and the letter ends by asking the readers to go out to him outside the camp, because "here we have no lasting city" and we seek the one to come (13:13–14). The Holy Sepulchre and Via Dolorosa notes use 13:12 for the location of the crucifixion; the point here is 13:14. The destination of Christian pilgrimage is a person who has gone ahead, not a place that holds him. Jesus said as much at the well (John 4:21–24).
## From text to practice

Three practices follow from the passage, not from willpower. First, confess the stranger status aloud: at the airport and at Taba, say Leviticus 25:23 together. Second, practise greeting from afar: at sites that disappoint, are crowded or are disputed, name what is not yet received, as the patriarchs did, without pretending. Third, keep Nebo in view: the last service is not an anticlimax but the shape of faith in this age, seeing the land and not entering it, because God has prepared a city. The ground of all three is verse 16.
stories.counterpoint: The strongest alternative reading holds that Hebrews 11 does not relativise the territorial promise at all. Genesis 17:8 calls the land an everlasting possession, and Romans 11:29 says God's gifts are irrevocable; on this view the heavenly country of verse 16 adds to the land promise rather than interpreting it, and the land of Israel keeps a distinct place in God's future. W. D. Davies' classic study The Gospel and the Land argued the opposite pole, that the New Testament largely transfers holy space onto the person of Christ. Hebrews' own vocabulary (city, foundations, Mount Zion, heavenly Jerusalem) favours fulfilment in a renewed creation, but the pilgrim should know that sincere Christians, including many who will be in Jerusalem at Christmas, read the land differently.
stories.why: This passage gives the group an identity before it gives them sites: guests in a land that belongs to God, travelling toward a city they have not seen. For the pastor it supplies the arc for the whole preaching load, from the departure gate to the Nebo service, and protects against both disappointment and spiritual tourism. It also reframes the TL's daily discipline as a form of the same faith: travelling together toward something not yet in hand.
questions: If Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner, what does it mean for this group to arrive there as guests?
Where will you need to greet a promise from afar on this trip rather than claim to have received it?
How would you preach Hebrews 13:14 at Nebo without making the land unimportant?

stories.headline: Five frontiers, three currencies, one headcount
stories.dek: The overture brief: how the twelve days are built, what papers each frontier wants, which calendar traps to plan around, and a script for the first bus.
body: The TL's weight sits at transitions. This trip has five frontiers (Jakarta to Dubai, Dubai to Cairo, Egypt to Israel at Taba, Israel to Jordan, Amman back to Dubai) and two all-night transits.
## How the twelve days are built

Egypt (Days 2 to 4) is long drives: Cairo to Dahab on Day 3 crosses the canal and runs most of the day, and Day 4 starts early for St Catherine's. Israel and Palestine (Days 5 to 9) is dense walking: the Old City on Day 7 is the longest, with steps and slick limestone; elderly pilgrims should be told now that a cane or walking pole is welcome. Jordan (Days 10 and 11) is the hardest physical day: a border crossing followed by Petra, where the walk from the visitor centre through the Siq to the Treasury is about two kilometres each way before anything else (horse carts and buggies exist for those who need them; confirm current prices on site). Then two transits. Ask Panorama for the list of pilgrims over 65 or with mobility limits.
## Papers at five frontiers
Status checked 24 November 2026; all of this must be rechecked with Panorama and official sites in the last week before departure.

Egypt: Canada's advice (updated 26 May 2026) notes visa on arrival is paid in US dollars cash and the amount reported varies; confirm whether Panorama is arranging a group e-visa for Indonesian passports.

Taba, Egypt to Israel: Australia's Smartraveller says the crossing is open but may close or restrict hours at short notice; Canada says the same. Indonesian passport holders need Israeli entry approval in advance; the Prep Hub notes a group visa. Ask Tephi who carries the approval letter and how many copies. Confirm whether the Egyptian exit fee and Israeli entry charges are prepaid. (The widely reported $120 Taba fee applies in the opposite direction, into Egypt.)

Bethlehem: the group sleeps in Palestinian-administered Bethlehem and drives to Jerusalem through Israeli checkpoints on Days 6 and 7. Passports must be on the body every day from Day 5 to Day 10, not in the hotel safe. This overrides the Prep Hub's site-day rule of leaving documents at the hotel.

Israel to Jordan: the northern crossing near Beit She'an (Jordan River / Sheikh Hussein) is the likely one from Galilee (hypothesis; confirm). Visit Jordan says Sheikh Hussein issues visas on arrival for most nationalities, Allenby and Wadi Araba do not, the Jordanian visa is 40 JOD unless covered by a group arrangement, and a 10 JOD departure tax applies at land crossings but not airports. Israeli exit fees at land borders are paid per person; confirm the current amount and whether Panorama prepays. Clocks go forward an hour.
## Calendar traps

Christmas Eve (Thursday) brings the Latin Patriarch's traditional procession from Jerusalem into Bethlehem and closes roads around Manger Square for parts of the day; plan the return from Jericho with that in mind. Christmas Day is Friday: Muslim Friday prayers fill the Old City around midday, and Jewish Shabbat begins at sunset, after which photography and phone use at the Western Wall plaza are not appropriate. Saturday 26 December is Shabbat: many Jewish-owned shops in Haifa and Tiberias close; Arab Nazareth stays open. Sunset is around 17:00 in Egypt and Israel, so outdoor sites belong in the morning.
## Money, handover and what goes wrong

Three currencies: Egyptian pounds, Israeli shekels (used in Bethlehem too) and Jordanian dinars, plus small US dollar notes for toilets and tips. Tipping is in the package; ask Panorama whether the TL hands out envelopes. Hawkers at Giza, Olivet and Petra: a polite, repeated no-thank-you without stopping is enough. On every service day Tesa takes the clock, the count and the phone while Merrick leads; agree before departure that during a service she can interrupt him with a single signal if the bus or border timing slips.

A pilgrim leaves a passport in the hotel safe on a checkpoint day: do a passport show-of-hands on the bus before departure from Bethlehem. A couple wanders off during free time at a market: give free time with an exact return time and a visible landmark, never "about twenty minutes". Pilgrims overheat at the Dead Sea and chill in Jerusalem the same day: announce layers the evening before. The group splits at a border queue: walk the group through as one body, with Tesa at the back.
## Two-minute briefing for the first bus in Cairo

"Good morning. Welcome to Egypt. Three things for twelve days. First, your number: everyone has one, and every time we get on the bus we count off out loud. The bus does not leave until the count is complete. Second, if you are lost, stand still and call or WhatsApp me or Tesa; do not look for us. Third, your passport and your participant card stay on your body every day; I will remind you each morning. We are guests in three countries and among Christians, Muslims and Jews who live here. Greet before you photograph, buy from local shops, and leave politics for home. And remember why we came. Abraham went out not knowing where he was going; you at least have a run sheet. Let's go."
## Fun facts
1. Melito of Sardis's Old Testament list, from about AD 170, omits Esther (Eusebius, Church History 4.26).
2. Gregory of Nyssa travelled to Jerusalem by the Roman imperial post, a government courier system, not as a private pilgrim (Letter 2).
3. Jerome notes that the hermit Hilarion, a native of the Gaza region, saw Jerusalem for only one day (Letter 58).
4. Jordan has not issued visas on arrival at the Wadi Araba crossing since 1 January 2016 (Visit Jordan).
5. Bethlehem's mayor put it in butcher's terms: when 10,000 visitors sleep in town, "the butcher is working" (Times of Israel, December 2025).
6. Renan sketched his Life of Jesus in a Lebanese village, Ghazir, during the summer after his mission.
stories.why: The overture is the cheapest moment to prevent the expensive mistakes: passports in safes on checkpoint days, unprepaid border fees, a Christmas Eve road closure nobody planned for. Settling the TL and pastor handover now protects Merrick's preaching days from logistics. The bus script turns the counting rule into something the group owns rather than resents.
questions: Which three questions for Tephi from this brief need an answer before the pre-departure briefing?
What single signal will Tesa use to interrupt a service if timing slips, and has she agreed to it?
Which pilgrims will need a seat near the front of the bus and a slower walking group from Day 2?
